section_1.title: The Visual Hook: The Inscribed Square Problem
section_1.content: Introduce the geometric puzzle: Given a closed continuous curve (like an ink splatter or a rubber band), can we always find four points on the curve that form the vertices of a square? Define the problem visually using a smooth, non-self-intersecting loop.
section_1.example: Visualize a cartoon character drawing a 'doodle' on a piece of paper; demonstrate how we can always find a square inside a simple circle, but ask if this holds for a 'wobbly' irregular shape.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Configuration Spaces
section_2.content: Explain that to solve this, we don't just look at the curve, but at the space of all possible pairs of points on the curve. Introduce the 'Configuration Space' as a 2D surface (a torus or triangle) representing all pairs (x, y) on the curve.
section_2.example: Use a grid animation where the x-axis represents the position of the first point and the y-axis represents the second; points on the curve are mapped to coordinates on this grid.

section_3.title: Mathematical Core: Symmetry and the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
section_3.content: Introduce the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem as the 'logical bridge.' Explain that for any continuous function from a sphere to a plane, there exist antipodal points that map to the same value. We apply this to the symmetry of squares to prove existence.
section_3.example: Show a visual of a sphere and its antipodal points; demonstrate how the 'square' constraint acts as a function that must 'hit zero' (find a perfect square) at some point on the curve.

section_4.title: The Proof Logic: Connecting Vertices
section_4.content: Explain the construction of the 'square function.' If we pick two points on the curve, the midpoint and the distance between them define a potential square. We show that the space of 'non-square' configurations is inconsistent, implying a square must exist.
section_4.example: An animation of a rotating square 'sweeping' through an irregular shape until it snaps perfectly onto four points on the perimeter.

section_5.title: Application & Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize that while the theorem holds for 'smooth' loops, it remains an open question for arbitrary non-smooth curves (Toeplitz's Conjecture). Discuss why topology provides certainty where geometric trial-and-error fails.
section_5.example: Final shot: A robot arm trying to find a square on an irregular wire loop; the math guarantees the arm will always succeed.

            "Consider a smooth, continuous, non-self-intersecting curve.",

        ])
        
        # Create a circle
        curve = Circle(radius=1.5, color="#FFFFFF")

        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.add(dots, quad)
        dots.add_updater(update_dots)
